tool.name: YAML
tool.tagline: The indentation-based data format behind most configuration files
tool.description: YAML is a human-friendly data serialization format used for Kubernetes manifests, CI pipelines, Docker Compose, Ansible and countless app configs. Learn its few structures, its string and typing rules and its traps, and every YAML-configured tool becomes easier to read and debug.

concepts.name: Mappings, sequences and indentation
concepts.summary: YAML has two collections: mappings of key: value pairs and sequences of - items, nested by indentation with spaces.
concepts.why: Every YAML file, from a CI pipeline to a Kubernetes manifest, is these two structures nested.
concepts.body:
A YAML document describes data built from three kinds of nodes: **mappings** (key/value pairs, like a dict or JSON object), **sequences** (ordered lists) and **scalars** (strings, numbers, booleans, null).

A mapping writes each pair as `key: value`, one per line. The space after the colon is required: `key:value` is a single string, not a pair.

A sequence writes each item on its own line after `- ` (dash and space).

**Indentation** shows nesting. Child nodes are indented more than their parent, using **spaces only**: tabs are not allowed for indentation. The amount is up to you (two spaces is the common style) but siblings must line up exactly.

A sequence that is the value of a mapping key may be indented or written at the same level as the key; both of these are valid and mean the same:

```yaml
steps:
  - build
  - test
steps2:
- build
- test
```

`#` starts a **comment** that runs to the end of the line; it must be preceded by whitespace when it follows a value.

Keys in one mapping must be unique, and mappings are unordered in the data model, although most parsers keep the file order.
concepts.code:
# a typical config file
name: web-app
version: 3
replicas: 2            # comments start with #
ports:
  - 80
  - 443
owner:
  team: platform
  email: platform@example.com
env:
- name: LOG_LEVEL      # a sequence of mappings
  value: info
- name: REGION
  value: eu-west-1

# parsed (as JSON):
# {"name": "web-app", "version": 3, "replicas": 2, "ports": [80, 443],
#  "owner": {"team": "platform", "email": "platform@example.com"},
#  "env": [{"name": "LOG_LEVEL", "value": "info"}, {"name": "REGION", "value": "eu-west-1"}]}
takeaways: key: value pairs form mappings; - item lines form sequences
Indent with spaces only; siblings must align
A space is required after the colon and the dash
pitfalls: Indenting with a tab, which is a syntax error in YAML even though it may look aligned in the editor.

quiz.q: How is the line image:nginx parsed inside a mapping?
options: As key image with value nginx
quiz.explain: Without a space after the colon it isn't a key/value separator, so it's a plain scalar.

concepts.name: Scalars: strings, numbers, booleans, null
concepts.summary: Unquoted scalars are typed automatically: 42 is an int, 3.5 a float, true a boolean, null or ~ is null, and almost everything else is a string.
concepts.why: Knowing how YAML guesses types prevents values from silently becoming the wrong type in your app.
concepts.code:
count: 42              # int
ratio: 0.75            # float
big: 1e6               # float 1000000.0 (a string in YAML 1.1 parsers)
enabled: true          # bool
nothing: ~             # null
empty:                 # null as well, not ""
blank: ""              # empty string
version: "3.10"        # string; unquoted 3.10 would be the float 3.1
zip: "01234"           # string; keeps the leading zero
region: eu-west-1      # string
mode: 0o644            # int 420 in YAML 1.2 (YAML 1.1 parsers want 0644)
takeaways: Plain scalars are typed by appearance: int, float, bool, null or string
Quote a value to force a string, e.g. version: "3.10"
An empty value is null, not an empty string
pitfalls: Writing python_version: 3.10, which parses as the float 3.1.

quiz.q: What is the value of key in key: (nothing after the colon)?
quiz.explain: A missing value is an empty node, which the schemas resolve to null.

concepts.name: Flow style and YAML as a superset of JSON
concepts.summary: Write compact inline collections with [a, b] and {k: v}, and know that (almost) any JSON document is already valid YAML.
concepts.why: Short lists read better inline, and knowing JSON is valid YAML helps when tools mix the two.
concepts.body:
Besides the indentation-based **block style**, YAML has a **flow style** borrowed from JSON:

- flow sequence: `[80, 443]`;
- flow mapping: `{cpu: 500m, memory: 1Gi}`.

Flow collections can nest and span several lines, and inside them indentation doesn't matter. Use them for short, simple values; long or deeply nested data is easier to read in block style.

In flow context the characters `,`, `[`, `]`, `{` and `}` are indicators, so a string containing them must be quoted inside a flow collection: `[a, "b,c"]`.

YAML 1.2 was designed so that **JSON is (nearly) a subset**: a JSON document is a valid YAML document with the same meaning. That's why tools that accept YAML usually accept JSON files too, and why you can paste a JSON snippet into a YAML file as a value.

The reverse isn't true: YAML adds comments, anchors, multi-line strings, unquoted strings and non-string keys that JSON can't express. When converting YAML to JSON, those features are resolved or lost.

Block and flow styles produce identical data; the choice is purely presentation.
concepts.code:
# block style
ports:
  - 80
  - 443
resources:
  cpu: 500m
  memory: 1Gi

# the same data in flow style
ports2: [80, 443]
resources2: {cpu: 500m, memory: 1Gi}

# quote strings with flow indicators inside flow collections
tags: [web, "env,prod", "[beta]"]

# a JSON document pasted in as a value is valid YAML
raw: {"id": 7, "labels": ["a", "b"], "ok": true}
takeaways: [a, b] and {k: v} are flow-style sequences and mappings
Block and flow styles describe exactly the same data
JSON is valid YAML 1.2; YAML adds comments, anchors and more
pitfalls: Leaving an unquoted comma in a value inside [ ], which splits it into two items.

options: Three items: a, b and c
quiz.explain: Inside a flow sequence a comma always separates items, with or without a space.

concepts.name: Multi-line strings: | and >
concepts.summary: Write long text with literal | (keeps newlines) and folded > (joins lines), and control the final newline with chomping indicators - and +.
concepts.why: Shell scripts in CI files, certificates and long descriptions all rely on block scalars.
concepts.body:
Block scalars hold multi-line text without escaping. They start with an indicator on the key's line, and the content is the indented lines below.

- **Literal** `|` keeps every line break exactly. Ideal for scripts, config snippets, PEM certificates.
- **Folded** `>` joins lines with spaces, turning each blank line into a newline. Ideal for long prose that you want to wrap in the source.

Both keep the text's relative indentation. The indentation of the first content line is stripped from all lines.

**Chomping** controls trailing newlines:

- default (clip): a single final newline;
- `|-` or `>-` (strip): no final newline;
- `|+` or `>+` (keep): all trailing newlines kept.

If the first line of content starts with spaces, give an explicit **indentation indicator**: `|2` means the content is indented two spaces relative to the parent.

In CI systems such as GitHub Actions, `run: |` is how you write multi-line shell steps. Note that `>` folding doesn't fold more-indented lines, which keeps code blocks inside folded text intact.

Inside block scalars nothing is special: `#`, `:`, quotes and backslashes are all literal text, which is exactly why they're convenient.
concepts.code:
script: |
  echo "building"
  make -j4
  # this is part of the string, not a YAML comment
description: >
  This long sentence is wrapped
  in the file but becomes one line.

  A blank line starts a new paragraph.
no_trailing_newline: |-
  value
keep_newlines: |+
  value

# parsed:
# script:  'echo "building"\nmake -j4\n# this is part of the string, not a YAML comment\n'
# description: 'This long sentence is wrapped in the file but becomes one line.\nA blank line starts a new paragraph.\n'
# no_trailing_newline: 'value'
# keep_newlines: 'value\n'   (plus any blank lines that followed)
takeaways: | keeps line breaks, > folds lines into spaces
Add - to drop the final newline, + to keep all trailing newlines
Everything inside a block scalar is literal text, including #
pitfalls: Using > for a shell script, which joins the commands into one line.

quiz.q: What string does this produce? key: |- followed by two indented lines a and b
quiz.explain: Literal style keeps the line break between lines, and the strip indicator removes the final newline.

concepts.name: Quoting: plain, single and double quotes
concepts.summary: Know when a string must be quoted, and the difference between single quotes (no escapes, '' for a quote) and double quotes (backslash escapes).
concepts.why: Unquoted special characters are the most common cause of YAML parse errors and wrong values.
concepts.body:
YAML has three **flow scalar** styles:

- **Plain** (unquoted): the most readable, no escapes, type is inferred.
- **Single-quoted** `'...'`: always a string, no escape sequences at all. A single quote inside is written twice: `'it''s'`. Backslashes are literal, which makes single quotes ideal for regexes and Windows paths.
- **Double-quoted** `"..."`: always a string, with backslash escapes: `\n`, `\t`, `\"`, `\\`, `\u00e9`, `\x41`. The only style that can represent any character, including control characters.

Quote a string when it:

- would be read as another type: `"yes"`, `"1.0"`, `"null"`, `"0123"`, `"2026-10-17"`;
- starts with an indicator: `*`, `&`, `!`, `|`, `>`, `%`, `@`, a backtick, `[`, `{`, `-` followed by a space, `?` or `:` followed by a space, or a quote;
- contains `: ` (colon space) or ` #` (space hash);
- has leading or trailing spaces you want to keep.

A practical rule: prefer plain style for ordinary words, single quotes when something needs quoting, and double quotes only when you need an escape like `\n`.

Plain scalars can contain `:` and `#` when they aren't followed or preceded by a space: `http://example.com#top` is fine unquoted.
concepts.code:
plain: hello world
url: http://example.com/a#frag      # fine: no ": " and no " #"
title: 'Note: read this'            # must quote, contains ": "
comment: 'a # b'                    # unquoted, " #" would start a comment
pattern: '^\d+\.\d+$'               # single quotes: backslashes are literal
path: 'C:\Users\ana'
its: 'it''s'                        # -> it's
escaped: "tab\there\nnew line"      # double quotes: escapes processed
unicode: "caf\u00e9"                # -> café
alias_like: '*not-an-alias'
answer: 'yes'                       # string, not a YAML 1.1 boolean
takeaways: Single quotes: no escapes, '' for a quote; double quotes: backslash escapes
Quote values containing ': ' or ' #', or starting with * & ! | > % @ [ {
Quote values that look like numbers, booleans, null or dates
pitfalls: Writing a regex like \d+ in double quotes, where \d is an invalid escape and fails to parse.

quiz.q: Which value parses to the string He said "hi"?
quiz.explain: Inside single quotes double quotes are ordinary characters; the double-quoted version would need \" escapes.

concepts.name: Anchors, aliases and merge keys
concepts.summary: Define a node once with &name and reuse it with *name, and merge mappings with <<: to share default settings.
concepts.why: They remove copy-paste from big config files such as CI pipelines and Docker Compose services.
concepts.body:
An **anchor** `&name` labels a node; an **alias** `*name` later in the same document refers to that same node. The parser expands it, so the resulting data contains the value twice (in many libraries literally the same object).

```yaml
defaults: &defaults
  retries: 3
  timeout: 30
job_a: *defaults
```

To reuse a mapping but override or add some keys, many parsers support the **merge key** `<<`:

```yaml
job_b:
  <<: *defaults
  timeout: 60
```

`job_b` gets `retries: 3` and its own `timeout: 60`; explicit keys win over merged ones. `<<: [*a, *b]` merges several, earlier ones taking precedence.

Caveats:

- The merge key was defined for YAML 1.1 and is **not part of YAML 1.2**. PyYAML, ruamel.yaml, Go's yaml.v3 and js-yaml support it, but some parsers and tools don't.
- Anchors work only within one document and must be defined before use.
- Aliases are expanded on load, so dumping the data back usually doesn't restore them.
- Tools like Docker Compose ignore top-level keys starting with `x-`, a convenient place to keep anchor definitions that aren't themselves config.
concepts.code:
x-defaults: &defaults          # x- keys are ignored by Docker Compose
  restart: unless-stopped
  logging:
    driver: json-file
  environment: &env
    TZ: UTC

services:
  api:
    <<: *defaults
    image: example/api:2.1
  worker:
    <<: *defaults
    image: example/worker:2.1
    restart: on-failure        # overrides the merged value
    environment: *env          # plain alias of a nested node

# worker parses to:
# {restart: on-failure, logging: {driver: json-file},
#  environment: {TZ: UTC}, image: example/worker:2.1}
takeaways: &name defines an anchor, *name reuses that node
<<: *anchor merges a mapping; explicit keys override merged ones
Merge keys are a YAML 1.1 feature, widely but not universally supported
pitfalls: Expecting an anchor defined in one document (or one file) to be available in another.

quiz.q: With base: &b {a: 1, b: 2} and c: {<<: *b, b: 3}, what is c?
quiz.explain: The merge supplies a and b, and the explicitly written key b: 3 takes precedence.

concepts.name: Multiple documents in one file
concepts.summary: Separate several YAML documents in one stream with ---, end one with ..., and load them all with a load_all style API.
concepts.why: Kubernetes manifests and many tools bundle several objects in one file this way.
concepts.body:
A YAML **stream** can contain several **documents**. A line containing just `---` starts a new document; `...` optionally marks the end of one. The first `---` is optional.

```yaml
kind: Service
---
kind: Deployment
```

Each document is independent: it has its own root node, and anchors don't carry over between documents.

Most libraries have two loading functions: one for a single document, which **fails** if the stream contains more, and one that returns all documents. In Python that's `yaml.safe_load` versus `yaml.safe_load_all`; in Go you call `Decode` repeatedly; `kubectl apply -f` reads them all.

`---` also appears at the top of many files that have just one document, simply as a start marker. A **directive** such as `%YAML 1.2` may precede it to declare the version, though few files use one.

Typical uses: several Kubernetes objects in one manifest, a log of records appended over time (`...` lets a reader know a document is complete), and front matter, where a Markdown file starts with a YAML document between `---` lines.

An empty document (two `---` in a row) loads as null, so filter out `None` values when iterating.
concepts.code:
# k8s.yaml: two Kubernetes objects in one file
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web
...

# Python:
#   import yaml
#   docs = list(yaml.safe_load_all(open("k8s.yaml")))
#   [d["kind"] for d in docs if d]      -> ['Service', 'Deployment']
#   yaml.safe_load(open("k8s.yaml"))    -> ComposerError: expected a single document
takeaways: --- separates documents in one stream; ... ends one
Use load_all style APIs to read every document
Anchors don't cross document boundaries
pitfalls: Calling a single-document loader on a multi-document manifest and getting an error.

quiz.q: A file has three documents separated by ---. What does PyYAML's safe_load do with it?
options: Raises an error because it expects a single document
quiz.explain: safe_load requires exactly one document; safe_load_all yields each one.

concepts.name: Implicit typing traps: the Norway problem
concepts.summary: Why NO, on, 012, 1:30 and 1e3 may not be what you think, how YAML 1.1 and 1.2 parsers differ, and how to stay safe.
concepts.why: Country codes turning into false and version numbers into floats are real production bugs.
concepts.body:
Implicit typing is convenient until a value that should be a string happens to look like something else. The infamous case is the **Norway problem**: a list of country codes where `NO` becomes `false`.

The rules depend on the YAML version the parser implements. Many popular parsers (PyYAML, older libyaml-based tools, Ruby's Psych, many Go v2 users) follow **YAML 1.1**, where:

- `yes`, `no`, `on`, `off`, `y`, `n` and their capitalised forms are booleans;
- `012` is octal (10), `0b101` binary, and `1_000` is 1000;
- `1:30` is a **sexagesimal** integer, 90;
- `2026-10-17` becomes a date object.

YAML 1.2's **core schema** is stricter: only `true`/`false` are booleans, octal needs `0o`, and sexagesimals and implicit dates are gone. Parsers implementing it include ruamel.yaml, Go's yaml.v3 (mostly), js-yaml 4 and the `yaml` npm package.

Some surprises exist in both: `1e3` is a float, `.5` is a float, `null` and `~` are null, and `3.10` is the float 3.1.

How to stay safe:

- **Quote** any string that could be read as something else: versions, codes, zip codes, times, IDs.
- Validate the loaded data against a schema so a wrong type fails loudly.
- Know which YAML version your tool's parser implements.
concepts.code:
# key           YAML 1.1 (PyYAML)     YAML 1.2 core schema
country: NO     # False                'NO'
switch: on      # True                 'on'
answer: yes     # True                 'yes'
mode: 0755      # 493 (octal)          755
time: 1:30      # 90 (base 60)         '1:30'
date: 2026-10-17  # date(2026,10,17)   '2026-10-17' (ruamel.yaml still gives a date)
python: 3.10    # 3.1                  3.1
build: 1e3      # '1e3' (1.1 needs a dot) 1000.0

# safe in every parser:
country_q: "NO"
version_q: "3.10"
takeaways: YAML 1.1 parsers treat yes/no/on/off as booleans and 012 as octal
YAML 1.2 core only has true/false and 0o octal
Quote codes, versions, times and IDs; validate types after loading
pitfalls: Assuming your parser follows YAML 1.2; PyYAML and many tools still implement 1.1.

quiz.q: With PyYAML, what does countries: [GB, NO, FR] load as?
quiz.explain: PyYAML implements YAML 1.1, where NO is a boolean.

concepts.name: Loading YAML safely in code
concepts.summary: Parse YAML with safe loaders (yaml.safe_load, not yaml.load with an unsafe Loader), limit alias expansion, and understand round-trip loaders.
concepts.why: YAML loaders can instantiate objects, so loading untrusted YAML unsafely is a remote-code-execution bug.
concepts.body:
YAML can carry **tags** that tell a loader to build language-specific objects, for example `!!python/object/apply:os.system`. A loader that honours them will run code chosen by whoever wrote the file. So:

- Python: use `yaml.safe_load` (or `yaml.load(s, Loader=yaml.SafeLoader)`), never `yaml.load` with `Loader=yaml.Loader` or `UnsafeLoader` on untrusted input. Since PyYAML 5.1, calling `yaml.load` without a `Loader` warns, and since 6.0 it is an error.
- Ruby: `YAML.safe_load`, the default for `YAML.load` since Psych 4.
- JavaScript: js-yaml 4 and the `yaml` package load only standard types by default.
- Java: SnakeYAML 2 uses a safe constructor by default; older code with `new Yaml()` was vulnerable.

Even safe loaders can be abused by **alias bombs** ("billion laughs"): a few lines with nested aliases that expand to billions of elements when the data is walked or serialized. Limit input size, and use parsers' alias limits where available (Go's yaml.v3 and the `yaml` npm package have them).

Some applications need to **edit** YAML while keeping comments and formatting. Normal loaders discard both. Use a round-trip library: `ruamel.yaml` in Python, the `yaml` package's Document API in JavaScript, yaml.v3 `Node` in Go.

For speed in Python, `yaml.CSafeLoader` uses libyaml and is many times faster.
concepts.code:
import yaml

doc = '''
name: demo
ports: [80, 443]
'''
print(yaml.safe_load(doc))          # {'name': 'demo', 'ports': [80, 443]}

evil = "!!python/object/apply:os.system ['echo pwned']"
try:
    yaml.safe_load(evil)
except yaml.constructor.ConstructorError as e:
    print("refused:", e.problem)    # refused: could not determine a constructor for the tag ...

from ruamel.yaml import YAML        # round-trip: comments survive
import sys
rt = YAML()
data = rt.load("replicas: 2  # keep this comment\n")
data["replicas"] = 3
rt.dump(data, sys.stdout)           # replicas: 3  # keep this comment
takeaways: Use safe_load (or the language's safe API) for any untrusted YAML
Alias bombs can blow up memory even with safe loaders: cap input size
Use round-trip libraries like ruamel.yaml to edit files and keep comments
pitfalls: Loading user-supplied YAML with yaml.load(..., Loader=yaml.Loader) or UnsafeLoader.

quiz.q: Why is yaml.load(data, Loader=yaml.UnsafeLoader) dangerous on untrusted input?
options: Tags in the input can make it construct arbitrary Python objects and run code
quiz.explain: Python-specific tags let the document call constructors such as os.system during loading.

concepts.name: Linting and schema validation
concepts.summary: Catch YAML mistakes early with yamllint for syntax and style, and JSON Schema for structure and types, in the editor and in CI.
concepts.why: Config errors found by a linter in seconds would otherwise surface as failed deploys.
concepts.body:
Two kinds of checks catch most YAML problems.

**Linting** checks syntax and style. `yamllint` reports indentation inconsistencies, duplicate keys, trailing spaces, overly long lines, truthy values like `yes` and `on` that should be quoted or written as `true`, and missing document starts. Configure rules in `.yamllint`; the `relaxed` preset is a gentle start.

**Schema validation** checks structure and types: required keys, allowed values, number ranges, string patterns. The common approach is **JSON Schema**, applied to the loaded data, since YAML and JSON share a data model.

- Editors: the YAML language server (VS Code's Red Hat YAML extension) validates and autocompletes against schemas, picking them from the **SchemaStore** catalog by filename (GitHub workflows, Compose files, many others) or from a `# yaml-language-server: $schema=...` comment at the top of the file.
- CI: `check-jsonschema` validates files on the command line; `kubeconform` validates Kubernetes manifests; `actionlint` checks GitHub Actions workflows.
- In code: load with a safe loader, then validate with a JSON Schema library or a typed model (Pydantic, for example).

Duplicate keys deserve special mention: many parsers silently keep the last value, so a duplicated `image:` deep in a manifest goes unnoticed. yamllint's `key-duplicates` rule catches it.
concepts.code:
# .yamllint
extends: default
rules:
  line-length: {max: 120}
  truthy: {allowed-values: ["true", "false"]}
  document-start: disable

# app.yaml
# yaml-language-server: $schema=./app.schema.json
name: web
replicas: two          # schema error: should be an integer
debug: yes             # yamllint: truthy value should be one of [true, false]
name: api              # yamllint: duplication of key "name" in mapping

# $ yamllint app.yaml
#   4:8   warning  truthy value should be one of [false, true]  (truthy)
#   5:1   error    duplication of key "name" in mapping  (key-duplicates)
# $ check-jsonschema --schemafile app.schema.json app.yaml   (once the duplicate is fixed)
#   app.yaml::$.replicas: 'two' is not of type 'integer'
takeaways: yamllint catches syntax, style, truthy values and duplicate keys
JSON Schema validates structure and types of the loaded data
Editors validate live via SchemaStore or a $schema comment
pitfalls: Relying on the parser to report duplicate keys; many keep the last one silently.

quiz.q: A manifest accidentally defines image: twice in one mapping. What do many parsers do?
options: Silently keep one value, often the last
quiz.explain: Duplicate keys are invalid per the spec but many parsers accept them; a linter catches them.

concepts.name: Tags and explicit types
concepts.summary: Use !!str, !!int and friends to force a type, understand local !tags used by tools like CloudFormation and Home Assistant, and how parsers map tags to types.
concepts.why: Tags explain both the explicit-typing escape hatch and the custom syntax many YAML-based tools invent.
concepts.body:
Every node in YAML has a **tag** that identifies its type. Usually the tag is resolved implicitly: plain `42` gets `tag:yaml.org,2002:int`. You can set it explicitly:

- **Standard tags** with the `!!` shorthand for `tag:yaml.org,2002:`: `!!str 123` is the string `"123"`, `!!float 1` is `1.0`, `!!int "7"`, `!!null`, `!!bool`. Also `!!map`, `!!seq`, and in YAML 1.1 `!!binary`, `!!timestamp`, `!!set`, `!!omap`.
- **Local tags** start with a single `!` and mean whatever the application decides. They are how tools extend YAML:
  - AWS CloudFormation: `!Ref MyBucket`, `!Sub "arn:aws:s3:::${Bucket}/*"`, `!GetAtt`.
  - Home Assistant: `!secret api_key`, `!include automations.yaml`.
  - GitLab CI: `!reference [.setup, script]`.

A generic parser that doesn't know a local tag either errors or returns a placeholder. Loading a CloudFormation template with plain `yaml.safe_load` fails on `!Ref`; you have to register a constructor for each tag (or use the tool's own library such as `cfn-flip`).

Registering constructors is also how you map tags to your own types in code, the safe counterpart of the `!!python/...` tags: you choose exactly which tags are allowed and what they build.

`%TAG` directives can define your own prefixes, but they are rarely used outside the spec.
concepts.code:
import yaml

print(yaml.safe_load("a: !!str 123\nb: !!float 1\nc: 123"))
# {'a': '123', 'b': 1.0, 'c': 123}

template = '''
Resources:
  Bucket:
    Type: AWS::S3::Bucket
Outputs:
  Name:
    Value: !Ref Bucket
'''
class Ref(str): pass

class CfnLoader(yaml.SafeLoader): pass
CfnLoader.add_constructor("!Ref", lambda loader, node: Ref(loader.construct_scalar(node)))

data = yaml.load(template, Loader=CfnLoader)
v = data["Outputs"]["Name"]["Value"]
print(type(v).__name__, v)          # Ref Bucket
# yaml.safe_load(template) -> ConstructorError: could not determine a constructor for the tag '!Ref'
takeaways: !!str, !!int, !!float force standard types
Single-! local tags are application-defined (CloudFormation !Ref, Home Assistant !secret)
Register a constructor per local tag on a safe loader to parse such files
pitfalls: Parsing a CloudFormation or Home Assistant file with a generic loader and getting unknown-tag errors.

quiz.explain: The explicit tag skips type resolution and keeps the scalar's text as a string.

concepts.name: Schemas: how plain scalars get their type
concepts.summary: Understand YAML's representation model: nodes, tags, and the failsafe, JSON and core schemas that resolve untagged scalars, and why parsers disagree.
concepts.why: This is the precise answer to every 'why did this value become a boolean/number/string?' question.
concepts.body:
YAML separates **syntax** from **data**. Parsing produces a **representation graph** of nodes (scalar, sequence, mapping), each with a tag. A plain scalar initially has the non-specific tag `?`; quoted and block scalars have `!`. **Tag resolution** then assigns real tags according to a **schema**:

- **Failsafe schema**: only `!!map`, `!!seq` and `!!str`. Every scalar is a string. Safe and predictable; some tools and config loaders can be set to it.
- **JSON schema**: plain scalars must match JSON forms exactly: `true`, `false`, `null`, JSON numbers. Anything else is an error rather than a string.
- **Core schema** (the YAML 1.2 recommendation): the JSON schema plus friendlier forms: `True`/`TRUE`, `Null`, `~`, empty values, `0o` octal, `0x` hex, `.inf`, `.nan`. Everything unmatched is a string.

Only `!`-tagged scalars (quoted or block style) are **always strings**; that's the formal reason quoting works.

YAML 1.1 had no schemas in this sense, only a list of "language-independent types" with regexes that included `yes/no/on/off`, sexagesimals, timestamps and `<<` merge. Most parsers' "default" behaviour is one of these schemas, possibly with extensions, which is why the same file loads differently across languages.

Many libraries let you choose: ruamel.yaml `typ="safe"` with version `(1, 1)` or `(1, 2)`, the npm `yaml` package's `schema: 'core' | 'json' | 'failsafe' | 'yaml-1.1'`, Go's yaml.v3 decoding into `string` fields.
concepts.code:
from ruamel.yaml import YAML

doc = "a: yes\nb: 0o17\nc: 017\nd: ~\ne: '42'\nf: 1:30\n"

y12 = YAML(typ="safe")              # YAML 1.2 core schema
print(y12.load(doc))
# {'a': 'yes', 'b': 15, 'c': 17, 'd': None, 'e': '42', 'f': '1:30'}

y11 = YAML(typ="safe")
y11.version = (1, 1)                # YAML 1.1 resolution rules
print(y11.load(doc))
# {'a': True, 'b': '0o17', 'c': 15, 'd': None, 'e': '42', 'f': 90}

# JavaScript, npm "yaml" package:
#   YAML.parse("a: yes\nb: 1", { schema: "failsafe" })  -> { a: 'yes', b: '1' }
takeaways: Plain scalars are typed by the schema; quoted and block scalars are strings
Failsafe: all strings; JSON: strict JSON forms; core: JSON plus friendly forms
YAML 1.1 rules differ, which is why parsers disagree
pitfalls: Assuming two parsers agree on a file's types; check which schema each one applies.

quiz.q: Under the YAML 1.2 failsafe schema, what is the type of the plain scalar 42?
quiz.explain: The failsafe schema has only map, seq and str, so every scalar resolves to a string.

concepts.name: Edge cases: complex keys, indentation, gotchas
concepts.summary: The corners experts know: ? complex keys, non-string keys, indentation of block sequences, tabs, BOMs, long keys and string folding in plain scalars.
concepts.why: These details explain the odd parse results and errors that remain once you know the basics.
concepts.body:
A few corners of the spec that come up in practice:

- **Keys needn't be strings.** `1: one` has an integer key, `true: x` a boolean one (in YAML 1.1, `on:` becomes `True`, famously breaking GitHub Actions' `on:` key in PyYAML-based tools). JSON conversion then stringifies or fails.
- **Complex keys**: `? ` introduces an explicit key, which can be a sequence or mapping. Python can't use a list as a dict key, so loaders may reject such documents.
- **Implicit keys** (without `?`) must fit on one line and are limited to 1024 characters.
- **Plain multi-line scalars** are allowed: a plain value may continue on more-indented lines, and the line breaks fold into spaces. This hides mistakes such as a forgotten `- ` that turns two list items into one string.
- **Indentation of sequences in mappings**: `key:` followed by `- item` at the same column is valid, because the `-` counts as indentation. But within one sequence all dashes must align.
- **Tabs** are forbidden for indentation but allowed as separation inside lines and inside quoted strings.
- **Byte order marks** are allowed only at the start of the stream; encodings must be UTF-8, UTF-16 or UTF-32.
- **Document markers in strings**: a line starting with `---` or `...` at column 0 inside a block scalar ends the document; indent it.
- **Duplicate keys** are invalid by the spec even though many parsers accept them.
concepts.code:
1: one                 # integer key
on: push               # YAML 1.1 parsers: key is the boolean True
? [lat, lon]           # complex key: a sequence
: point
items:
- first
- second
  third                # not a new item: continues "second" -> 'second third'
message: |
  a line
  --- indented, so it is text, not a document marker

# PyYAML (YAML 1.1) loads the first two keys as 1 and True, and
# fails on the complex key: "found unhashable key"
takeaways: Keys can be numbers, booleans or even collections
Plain scalars can continue on indented lines, hiding missing dashes
Lines starting with --- or ... at column 0 end a document, even in a block scalar
pitfalls: Dropping the - on a list item so it silently becomes part of the previous item's string.

quiz.q:
In the YAML below, how many items does the list have?
- a
- b
  c
quiz.explain: The more-indented line c continues the plain scalar b, giving the items 'a' and 'b c'.
